title: Every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3–14)
hookLine: a long sentence of praise: chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed
carry: to the praise of his glory
tomorrow: Paul prays for friends. what does he ask for, if not a fix?
last: IN DUE SEASON WE SHALL REAP.

lines: BLESSED BE THE GOD AND FATHER.
cards: A blessing over a cup of coffee sounds like a lot, until you know the habit behind it.
In Jewish tradition there are blessings for bread, for wine, for fruit, even for thunder, and one for ordinary things like a drink: by whose word all things came to be.
Each begins, in English, Blessed are you, Lord our God. Now open Ephesians.
Its first words: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ." Some readers hear the same shape.

teach.h: WHAT DO YOU DO WITH A GOOD THING?
teach.b: Today's question: what do you do with a good thing? Paul's answer is to say so, to God, and he can't stop. Some readers take verses three to fourteen as one long Greek sentence, gift piled on gift.
Chosen: "he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world." Adopted, the word from three days ago. Redeemed: "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins."

Sealed with the Holy Spirit, a deposit on what's still to come. And under it all, a refrain like a chorus: "to the praise of his glory." The neighbor next door has the same instinct, in its own words.
In the Talmud, Rabbi Meir teaches that a person should say a hundred blessings every day. That's the thing to tell a friend tonight.
A hundred means noticing bread, water, waking up, the first fruit of a season, a storm rolling in. Shared ground, and it's wide: Jews and Christians both answer good things by blessing God for them.

teach.h: TO THE PRAISE OF HIS GLORY.
teach.b: Paul's blessing runs through Jesus; every gift in his list comes "in Christ." Jewish blessings bless God as King of the universe, and Judaism does not share the Christian faith in Jesus as the Messiah.
One habit of thanks, two traditions, and a real difference neither needs to hide.

how: Christians say grace before meals and praise God in hymns and doxologies; some churches sing or read Ephesians 1:3 as a call to worship.

a lucky streak of money and good health

s: a rabbi in the Talmud urges a hundred blessings a day
Rabbi Meir, in tractate Menachot: a habit of noticing gifts all day.
Jewish blessings and Paul's blessing are the same, word for word
shared habit, honest difference: Paul blesses in Christ; Jewish blessings bless God as King of the universe.
Ephesians opens with the words blessed be the God and Father
a blessing first, before any request or argument.

games.q: your cousin posts a new car with '#blessed' and says Ephesians 1:3 promised it. what does Paul's list of blessings actually name?
o: chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed: spiritual blessings, in Christ.
health and wealth for the people who pray hardest.
a reward for good behavior, paid out in this life.
games.why: Paul says all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ, then names them: chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed. his answer to all of it is praise.

practice: Count your blessings slowly, on your fingers: something you ate today, someone who spoke to you, something you saw. Give each one a full breath before you move to the next.
If you pray, you can close each with Paul's refrain: to the praise of his glory.

wordCard.voice: Every spiritual blessing. The opening of Ephesians: chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed, poured out in one long rush of praise.

orig.note: Greek: blessed, the first word of Ephesians 1:3, the opening shape of a blessing.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: to the praise of his glory, the chorus under every gift. Be well.
